topics: 🔏 A Slave's Seal — may he go out with a chotam on Shabbat, and where?
🐴 Ornament or Burden? — why animals may never go out with a seal or bell
🔔 The Bell's Clapper — what makes a zog a 'vessel' susceptible to impurity
🚪 Door-Bell to Animal-Bell — vessels fall into impurity by thought, rise out only by an act
🛠️ Detached but Connected — Abaye and Rava on a bell whose clapper was removed

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Slaves' Seals, Animals' Bells, and What Makes a Vessel Impure
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 58a–58b
overview.hebrewSource: יוֹצֵא הָעֶבֶד בְּחוֹתָם שֶׁבְּצַוָּארוֹ אֲבָל לֹא בְּחוֹתָם שֶׁבִּכְסוּתוֹ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues the mishna's list of items one may not wear into the public domain on Shabbat, focusing on a slave's identifying seal (chotam). The Gemara reconciles Shmuel's ruling — permitted around the neck, forbidden on the clothes — with contradictory baraitot, first via who made the seal and then via whether it is metal or clay. It contrasts this with an animal, for which any such item is a burden rather than an ornament and is always forbidden. The discussion then turns to ritual impurity: a bell (zog) is a 'vessel' only when it has a clapper (inbal) that lets it sound, a principle traced to a verse about metal implements. The daf closes with Abaye and Rava disputing why a bell whose clapper was removed keeps its earlier impurity, drawing in the laws of jointed tools like scissors and a carpenter's plane.

slides.title: 🔏 Shmuel's Seal — Neck Yes, Clothes No
slides.subtitle: Two contradictions, two resolutions

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Shmuel: a slave may go out with a seal שֶׁבְּצַוָּארוֹ (around his neck) but not one שֶׁבִּכְסוּתוֹ (on his clothes). Yet a baraita forbids both!

lines.speaker: Answer 1
lines.text: Not difficult: the baraita permitting the neck-seal means his master made it — the slave won't dare remove it. The baraita forbidding it means he made it himself, so he might remove and carry it.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Then why forbid a master-made seal on the clothes? He wouldn't remove that one either!

lines.speaker: Answer 1
lines.text: It might snap off; in fear of his master he'd fold his cloak onto his shoulders to hide the gap — and a folded cloak carried on the shoulders makes one liable for a sin-offering (Rabbi Yoḥanan).

lines.speaker: Alt. view
lines.text: Rav Naḥman (Rabba bar Avuh): both baraitot speak of a master-made seal. The real difference is metal (forbidden — the master is particular about it) versus clay (permitted — he is not).

lines.speaker: Proof
lines.text: The baraita adds 'both cannot become impure' — that only teaches something novel for metal seals, since stone, dung, and unfired earthenware never contract impurity to begin with.

callout.label: Conclusion:
callout.text: The metal/clay reading wins: it alone explains why the baraita bothers to note that these seals cannot become ritually impure.

slides.title: 🐴 What May Go Out on Shabbat — Person vs. Animal
slides.subtitle: The same items, different rules
rows: Permitted — fear of his master keeps it on
Forbidden — might snap and be carried
Forbidden — always a burden, never an ornament
Forbidden — might snap and be picked up
Permitted — 'anything woven into the garment, the Sages did not decree against' (Rav Huna b. Rav Yehoshua)
Forbidden — same reasoning as the animal's seal

callout.label: Why animals differ:
callout.text: For a person a seal or bell can be an ornament; for an animal, the Gemara says, these items are considered burdens it carries, not adornments — so they are barred outright, regardless of the neck/clothes distinction that applies to people.

slides.title: 🔔 A Bell Is Only a 'Vessel' If It Can Sound
slides.subtitle: The clapper (inbal) decides ritual impurity

boxes.title: Has a Clapper
items: Bells for a mortar, a cradle, Torah-scroll mantles, children's coverings — impure
Derived from Numbers 31:23: 'every davar' includes dibbur (something that 'speaks') — a metal sound-making vessel is impure (R' Shmuel bar Naḥmani, R' Yonatan)

boxes.title: No Clapper
items: Child's bell — pure; it exists only to make sound, so silent = not a vessel

boxes.title: Exception
items: An adult's bell — impure even with no clapper, since for an adult it is an ornament in itself
Once impure, removing the clapper does NOT purify it (see next slide)

slides.title: 🚪 A Door's Bell, an Animal's Bell
slides.subtitle: Vessels fall into impurity by thought, but rise out only through an actual change

nodes.content: ❓ Baraita: a door's bell is pure (it is like the house — attached to the ground); an animal's bell is impure. But another source calls an animal's bell pure!
🔑 Resolved: that second source means a bell with no clapper — silent bells are not vessels at all

columns.label: Door's bell → made into an animal's bell
columns.content: Becomes impure — it now has a new, sound-producing use

columns.label: Animal's bell → made into a door's bell
columns.content: STAYS impure, even nailed permanently into the door

nodes.content: 📜 Principle: כׇּל הַכֵּלִים יוֹרְדִין לִידֵי טוּמְאָתָן בְּמַחְשָׁבָה, וְאֵין עוֹלִין מִידֵּי טוּמְאָתָן אֶלָּא בְּשִׁנּוּי מַעֲשֶׂה — vessels FALL into impurity through mere intent (designation); they RISE out of it only through an actual physical change

slides.title: 🛠️ A Clapperless Bell — Still Impure?
slides.subtitle: Abaye and Rava debate a detached part

steps.content: 1️⃣ Tosefta: bells for a mortar, cradle, Torah-scroll mantle, or children's covering — if the clapper is later removed, the bell's earlier impurity remains
2️⃣ Question: without a clapper it seems useless — why isn't it simply 'broken' and purified?
3️⃣ Abaye: an ordinary person, not only a craftsman, can pop the clapper back in — so it is never truly 'broken'

4️⃣ Rava objects, from a baraita: jointed scissors and a detachable plane-blade are a 'connection' לַטּוּמְאָה (for impurity) but NOT a connection לַהַזָּאָה (for sprinkling the purification waters) — whichever way that word is read, Abaye's bell case does not match

5️⃣ Rabba: by Torah law, parts are 'connected' only while assembled and in use; the Sages then fenced in both directions — always connected for impurity, never connected (even in use) for sprinkling. But this leaves Abaye's bare, unused bell unexplained — so Rava sets out to answer differently, continuing onto the next amud

summary.principle: A slave's or animal's item is judged by two questions — will fear of the master keep it in place, and does it truly serve as an ornament — while a bell counts as a ritually susceptible vessel only through its capacity to sound, a status it can gain by designation but loses only through actual physical change.

flowSteps.content: 🔏 Slave's seal: permitted around the neck, forbidden on the clothes (fear of loss → carrying)
🐴 For an animal, any seal or bell is a burden, not an ornament — always forbidden

columns.content: 🔔 Bell impure only with a clapper (sound) — except an adult's bell, an ornament regardless
🚪 Door-bell repurposed → impure; impurity never lost by mere re-designation

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: vessels descend into impurity through thought alone, but ascend from it only through an actual change to the object

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, where may a slave go out on Shabbat with his identifying seal?
o: On his clothes
Around his neck
On his shoes
Nowhere at all
quiz.e: Shmuel ruled that a slave may go out with a seal around his neck, but not with one on his clothes.

quiz.q: Why is a seal on a slave's clothes forbidden even when his master made it for him?
o: Because clothes-seals are always impure
Because it might snap off, and in fear he might fold his cloak onto his shoulders and carry it
Because only free men may wear seals on clothes
Because the mishna never mentions clothes
quiz.e: The concern is that the seal could become detached; fearing his master's reaction, the slave might fold up his cloak and carry it on his shoulders, which Rabbi Yoḥanan says makes one liable for a sin-offering.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara say a seal or bell on an ANIMAL is always forbidden on Shabbat, unlike for a slave?
o: Animals cannot legally own property
For an animal these items are considered a burden it carries, not an ornament
Animal bells are always impure
It is only a custom, not a real prohibition
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that for an animal, a seal or bell has the status of a burden rather than an ornament, so it is forbidden regardless of where it is placed.

quiz.q: What makes a bell (zog) a 'vessel' susceptible to ritual impurity, according to the Gemara's derivation from Numbers 31:23?
o: Being made of gold specifically
Having a clapper that lets it produce sound — 'every davar' is read to include dibbur, something that 'speaks'
Being owned by a priest
Being attached to a door
quiz.e: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani cited Rabbi Yonatan: a metal object that produces sound is included in the verse's 'every article,' read homiletically to include dibbur (speech/sound), and so can become ritually impure.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, why does a bell whose clapper was removed retain its earlier ritual impurity instead of becoming pure?
o: Because metal can never become pure again
Because an ordinary person, not only a craftsman, can put the clapper back in, so it is not considered truly broken
Because the Sages made a decree specifically for this case with no reason given
Because the clapper itself was never impure
quiz.e: Abaye holds that a vessel is only considered 'broken' (and thus purified) when reassembling it requires a craftsman's expertise; since anyone can reinsert a clapper, the bell is not broken and its impurity persists.
